intros.market: Five CAs control 92.4% of all trusted certificate issuance, led by Internet Security Research Group at 39.2% and Google Trust Services at 20.9%. The top three CAs account for 75.5% of the market (CR3), while 75 smaller CAs share the remaining 7.6% of issuance. The market HHI of 2,369 indicates high concentration just below the threshold typically flagged by antitrust regulators, with 89 total trusted CAs competing in a system where dominance is heavily skewed toward automation-first providers.
intros.trust: 335 trusted roots are distributed across four major root programs, but only 90 roots appear in all four stores simultaneously. Microsoft maintains 142 roots not present in Chrome, Mozilla, or Apple, creating significant store disagreement that forces CAs to maintain multiple validation paths. Only 38 CA organizations are included in all four root programs, meaning most CAs face browser-specific trust limitations. This fragmentation compounds the concentration risk seen in market share, as only the largest CAs can reliably maintain universal browser trust.
intros.conc: The market HHI of 2,369 signals high systemic concentration, with three CAs controlling three-quarters of all issuance and five CAs controlling 92.4%. A single-point failure at Internet Security Research Group or Google Trust Services would impact 60% of the web's certificate infrastructure. This concentration creates efficiency but couples global HTTPS availability to the operational resilience of a handful of organizations, most of which are US-based.
intros.tail: 75 CAs operate in the long tail with minimal issuance volume yet retain full inclusion in at least one major root program. These CAs collectively account for only 7.6% of issuance but represent 84% of the CA population, creating asymmetric governance burden for root programs that must monitor dozens of low-volume operators. The tail contributes disproportionately to incident counts while serving niche markets that larger CAs often ignore.
intros.geo: US-based CAs issue 92% of all trusted certificates despite representing only 15 of 85 total certificate authorities. Europe hosts 44 CAs but accounts for just 7.9% of issuance, while Asia-Pacific's 17 CAs contribute only 0.09%. This geographic concentration mirrors the market share concentration, as the top five CAs are all US-incorporated entities operating under US legal jurisdiction.
intros.gov: 30 government-operated or state-owned CAs hold trusted status across root programs but collectively issue only 0.07% of certificates. These CAs span multiple regions including China, India, Turkey, and several European nations, creating geographically distributed but low-volume state surveillance surface. Despite minimal issuance share, their presence in root stores grants state actors cryptographic authority over HTTPS interception within their jurisdictions.
intros.jurisdiction: Five jurisdictions are classified as high-risk for compelled disclosure or interception mandates: China, Russia, the United Kingdom, Australia, and Hong Kong. India and Turkey are categorized as moderate-risk based on legal frameworks that permit government access to cryptographic systems. These classifications intersect with the 30 government-operated CAs to create legal and technical vectors for state-level HTTPS compromise, independent of actual issuance volume.
intros.ops: 1,562 total incidents have been recorded across 54 CAs, with misissuance (607 incidents) and governance failures (503) representing 71% of all events. CAs self-reported only 26% of incidents, while external researchers discovered 18% and automated tools found 17%, indicating weak internal controls. 193 incidents involved policy failures and 139 involved disclosure failures, with only 8% discovered through the audit process that theoretically provides third-party oversight.
intros.crypto: Root certificate cryptographic posture has largely migrated to RSA 4096-bit and ECDSA P-384 keys, with SHA-256 signatures now standard across active issuance hierarchies. 37 CAs maintain active TLS issuance capability, with median certificate validity usage at 66 days well below the current 398-day browser limit. Nine CAs have deployed ETSI-compliant infrastructure using the EN 319 411-1 v3.5 standard, while the majority rely on WebTrust audit frameworks.
intros.distrust: 16 distrust events have occurred across the CA ecosystem, with 14 attributed to compliance or operational failures rather than cryptographic compromise. Negligent noncompliance accounts for 7 cases, while 3 involved demonstrated incompetence and 3 involved willful circumvention of requirements. Root programs grant a median runway of 1,185 days (3.2 years) between distrust announcement and full removal, and 10 of the 16 events involved CAs with a documented pattern of repeated issues.
intros.policy: 43 active TLS CAs face a March 2026 deadline requiring certificates under 200 days validity, yet 3 remain at risk and 5 are vulnerable to the March 2027 100-day limit based on actual replacement behavior. The 47-day limit arriving in March 2029 sees only 8 CAs ready today, with a median observed validity period of 66 days. This compliance challenge unfolds against a regulatory surface that has grown 121x since 2000 to 6,664 total obligations spanning CA/B Forum baseline requirements, four root programs, and multiple audit standards, with 76% of obligations now mandatory and zero new ballots passed since 2022 despite mounting complexity.
intros.governance: Chrome commented substantively on 18.4% of the 223 incidents reported in 2025, down from 67.8% coverage in 2019 when 255 incidents occurred. Mozilla's substantive coverage dropped from 78% to 9.9% over the same period, while Apple engaged on 5.4% and Microsoft on 0% of incidents. This declining oversight occurs as the bug corpus reaches 1,848 total incidents across 818 Mozilla bugs and 730 Chrome bugs, with only 112 recent Chrome substantive comments and 47 from Mozilla despite ongoing CA compliance failures.
intros.community: 56 organizations hold CA/B Forum membership but only 21 actively contribute to ballot work, leaving 35 members with zero recorded contributions. Sectigo leads organizational participation while Stephen Davidson has proposed 36 ballots and endorsed 1, representing the most active individual contributor. This imbalance means a small minority shapes the standards that all 89 trusted CAs must follow, with the silent majority of members consuming policy without contributing to its development.
intros.audit: Auditors identified only 32% of the 414 in-scope incidents that occurred during their audit periods, with 132 caught and 282 missed despite clean opinions issued. 38 CAs show high transparency gaps between audit letter dates and public disclosure, while 5 CAs received qualified opinions and 11 changed auditors in 2025. WebTrust self-reporting reached 59.1% and ETSI self-reporting 66.4%, but auditor quality scores vary widely from BDO's 55.9 average to TayllorCox's 84.6, with auditor market concentration (HHI 541) far lower than CA market concentration. The top five auditors include KPMG with 11 CAs, Deloitte and BDO with 7 each, and gaps averaging 73 to 100 days between audit periods and public letters.
